l: miser, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The miser is an evil, stingy person unsuited to riches. He denies himself bread and enjoyment, hoarding goods that others will later revel in. His covetous eye is never satisfied, and wicked injustice dries up his soul, leaving him grudging even to himself.

l: man who meditates on wisdom, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A man who meditates on wisdom is pronounced blessed. He reasons with understanding, considers her ways, gains knowledge of her secrets, then lingers at her paths, windows and doors, pitches his tent near her, and shelters his children beneath her branches from heat.

l: my son, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A son addressed in Chapter 14 is advised to treat himself well according to his means and bring worthy offerings to the Lord. He is urged to do good to friends, enjoy a good day, give and take, before dying and leaving his labors to another.

l: Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The Lord is portrayed across these records as the eternal God and King of all, addressed as Father, Master, Savior, protector and helper. He sees all human ways and secret places with eyes ten thousand times brighter than the sun, and knew all things before creation and after completion. His working and mercy are from everlasting. The records begin with attributes of knowledge and fatherhood: the speaker begs not to be abandoned to adversaries and calls on the Father of his Lord. Fear of him is praised as better than riches and strength, greater than finding wisdom, and a covering more than any glory; harmony among kindred, neighbors and spouses is beautiful before him. He relates to Israel, likened to a firstborn, and has his sanctuary in Jerusalem. A petition asks him to show mercy, work new signs, remember his oath, gather the tribes of Jacob, fill Zion with glory, and reward those who wait for him, so all the earth will know he is the eternal God. He created physician and medicines, gives men skill so he is glorified in his works, and heals the sick who pray. History shows him creating glory in famous men, pleased with Enoch, making everlasting covenants with Noah, and assuring Abraham by oath that nations would be blessed through his offspring. He is worshipped through Simon's offering, with people worshipping and singers praising him as the God who does great things, exalts days from the womb, and deals according to mercy. The records end with the narrator's thanks: he delivered the speaker from destruction, slander, enemies and fire, gave a tongue as a reward, and will reward those who work in his time and wait for him.

l: sinners, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: sees wisdom (personified as she) [negated: will not see her] Sinners will not see wisdom, and foolish men will not obtain her, while liars will not remember her. Praise is not attractive in a sinner's mouth because it was not sent to him from the Lord. Sinners are not to excuse themselves by blaming the Lord, who has no need of a sinful man.

l: free choice, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: enables keeping the commandments [faithfulness is a matter of choice] Free choice is presented as the basis of human responsibility: if a person chooses, he can keep the commandments, and faithfulness is a matter of his choice. The Lord set fire and water, life and death, before man, and whichever he likes will be given to him. This is why no one may say the Lord caused him to fall away or err.

l: man, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Man was made by the Lord from the beginning and left with free choice in his own counsel. He may reach for life or death, receiving whichever he likes. The Lord knows every act but commands no one to be ungodly or licenses sin.

l: abomination, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Abomination is wickedness: knowledge of it is not wisdom, sinners' prudence is no counsel, and those who rejoice in it face condemnation (Chapter 19).

l: ungodly children, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Ungodly children are portrayed as unprofitable and not to be desired or trusted in for their numbers. Chapter 16 argues one child beats a thousand, childlessness beats ungodly offspring, and wicked races become desolate while one understanding person populates a city.

l: sinners, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Sinners are a disobedient, stiff-necked group: fire and wrath are kindled among them, they cannot escape with plunder or go unpunished, and their belief that they can hide from the Lord among many is rebuked.

l: creation, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: is boundless Creation is described as boundless, yet heaven, the heaven of heavens, the deep, and the earth will be moved when the Lord visits, and the mountains and the earth's foundations tremble at his look. The Lord arranged it from the beginning, and after this he filled the earth with his blessings, so that all manner of living things covered its surface and return into it.

l: works of the Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The Lord's works are described as ordered by his judgment from the beginning, with boundaries set at their making and arrangement for all time and generations. They are full of his glory, obedient, never hungry, weary, or disobedient, and do not crowd one another. Most remain hidden like an unseen tempest, and even the saints cannot declare them all. They endure in many uses, exist in opposing pairs, and nothing is added or diminished; none is imperfect.

l: divine judgment, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: has_boundaries_set his works [determined from their making] The Lord judges a man according to his works, and each man will receive according to his works. Past examples include the giants, Lot's neighbors, the people of perdition, and the six hundred thousand footmen. The text rejects the idea that anyone can hide from this judgment or go unremembered, and notes that the Lord's covenant and righteous works are hard to comprehend and seem afar off.

l: mankind, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Mankind is made from earth and returns to it, formed in the Lord's image with numbered days. Humans hold authority over beasts and birds and are given counsel, senses, and knowledge of good and evil. They receive a law of life and a covenant, and are urged to avoid unrighteousness, treat neighbors rightly, and praise the Lord while alive. Yet they are limited, mortal, prone to evil, and finally earth and ashes.

l: Israel, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Israel is the people called by the Lord's name, his portion and firstborn-like inheritance, composed of the tribes of Jacob. It is first named as the place of Wisdom's inheritance. A prayer pleads for mercy and for the tribes to be gathered. Moses received the law to teach them, and Aaron and the priesthood blessed and enlightened them, with Phinehas atoning for them. Joshua gave them their inheritance, and only he and Caleb of six hundred thousand entered the promised land. David received a glorious throne in Israel. After Solomon the kingdom divided, Jeroboam led Israel into sin, and its people were removed from their land.

l: sins and unrighteousness, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: is_known_to The Lord [not hidden, all before him] The Lord warns mankind to beware of all unrighteousness, and the text states that iniquities and sins are never hidden from him but are all before him. He will repay people for their deeds. People are told to forsake sins, turn away from iniquity and greatly hate the abominable thing, and flesh and blood are said to devise evil.

l: repentance and mercy, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The topic concerns repentance and mercy: the Lord grants a return to those who repent and comforts the hopeless. Chapter 17 urges turning back, forsaking sins, and praying with fewer offenses, marvels at his great mercy and forgiveness, and notes only the living, not the dead, can praise him.

l: mankind, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Mankind is a short-lived collective, living at most a hundred years, likened to a drop of water or pebble against eternity. Questioned about purpose, good and evil, it faces an evil end, yet the Lord shows patience, mercy and forgiveness; inquiry into God's works leaves man perplexed at the beginning.

l: mercy, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Mercy is contrasted by scope: human mercy reaches a neighbor, while the Lord's covers all flesh through reproving, chastening, teaching, and shepherd-like return. Prompted by human brevity and evil, he multiplies forgiveness, favoring those who accept chastening and seek his judgments.

l: word and gift, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Advice from a speaker to his son on giving: don't mar good deeds with reproach or harsh words. A kind word is better than a gift, like dew on heat; a gracious person offers both, while fools and grudging givers spoil giving.

l: wisdom, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: is_known_by every man of understanding A wise man is cautious in everything and beware of offense even in days of sinning, and every man of understanding knows wisdom and gives thanks to the one who found her. Those who understood sayings became wise and poured out apt proverbs. The chapter also counsels learning before speaking, self-examination before judgment, and repentance in the time of sins.

l: self-restraint and desires, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Counsel on self-restraint: don't follow lusts, restrain appetites. Fully indulging the soul's desire makes one an enemies' laughing stock. The chapter closes warning against luxurious banquets on borrowed money, which leaves one a beggar with an empty purse.

l: gossip, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: is_like arrow stuck in thigh [in a fool] Gossip is compared to an arrow stuck in the thigh when it lodges in a fool. The text advises never repeating what is heard, and says one who hates gossip has less wickedness.

l: fool, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A fool, lacking wisdom, is portrayed as someone who agonizes over a heard word like a woman in labor, with gossip lodged in him like an arrow in the thigh.

l: friend, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A friend should be questioned before being believed guilty, since he may not have done it, or may stop if he did. The text warns that slander is common and not every word should be trusted.

l: neighbor, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A neighbor should be questioned about what he is said to have said, since he may not have said it or may not repeat it. He should be reproved before being threatened, giving place to the law of the Most High.

l: wisdom, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Wisdom is defined as the fear of the Lord and its fulfilment, containing the doing of the law. Chapter 19 excludes knowledge of wickedness or sinners' prudence from wisdom; Chapter 21 adds that grace lies on the wise's lips, while to a fool wisdom is like a destroyed house.

l: sinners, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Sinners are portrayed as lacking true counsel despite their prudence. They suffer sevenfold more calamities than all creatures, such as death, strife, famine and plague, which were created for the wicked and caused the flood; their goods and children prove fragile.

l: deceitful man, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A deceitful man outwardly mourns, head hung low and feigning deafness, while inwardly full of deceit. He exploits strangers where unknown, and though lack of power may restrain him, he does mischief whenever opportunity arises.

l: wise man, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The wise man is silent until his time has come, then speaks wisely, becoming beloved, advancing himself, and pleasing great men when prudent. Yet favors and gifts can blind him and muzzle his reproofs, and hidden wisdom profits nothing.

l: fool, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The fool, paired with the braggart, mistimes his speech: his parables are rejected, his pleasantries wasted. His gifts bring no profit because he expects manifold repayment, gives little, insults much, and lends only to demand back. He complains of having no friend or thanks, and ends laughed to scorn by many.

l: liar, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The continual liar is portrayed as an ugly blot on a person, common among the ignorant; though a thief also inherits destruction, the liar is worse, destined for dishonor and constantly accompanied by shame.

l: silence, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: is_a mark of wisdom or of lacking an answer [varies by person] Silence is shown to have different meanings: one person is silent because he has no answer, while another is silent knowing when to speak and is found wise. A wise man is silent until his time has come, and some people are kept from sinning or are troubled less through lack and rest.

l: gifts, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Gifts are a proverbial topic: they vary in profit, some yielding nothing, others repaying double, while a fool's gift is worthless; favors and gifts blind the wise and muzzle reproofs.

l: sin (Chapter 21), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Sin, in Chapter 21, is a topic portrayed through two images: a snake to flee, whose lion-like teeth slay souls, and a two-edged sword whose stroke cannot heal.

l: son (the speaker's son), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: is_instructed_to sin no more [and ask forgiveness for past sins] The speaker addresses his son and asks whether he has sinned. He is told to sin no more and to ask forgiveness for his past sins.

l: fool (Chapter 21), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The fool is portrayed as an empty, careless figure: his inward parts are a broken vessel holding no knowledge, he discards wise words, laughs loudly, rushes into houses, and speaks heedlessly; his chatter burdens others, and instruction feels like fetters to him.

l: wise man (Chapter 21), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The wise man of Chapter 21 is a prudent, clever figure whose knowledge abounds like a flood, with counsel like a fountain of life. His words are sought and weighed, his mouth reflects his heart, and he smiles quietly, grieves at disgrace, and treasures instruction.

l: sinners, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: has_way_ending_in Hades [way paved with stones] The way of sinners is paved with stones, and at its end is the pit of Hades. One who hates reproof is on the path of the sinner, and the congregation of wicked men is like a bundle of tow with a flame at its end.

l: slothful man, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A slothful man in Chapter 22 is likened to a defiled stone and a dunghill's filth; disgraced, everyone hisses at him, and anyone lifting him shakes him off.

l: fool, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The fool is a figure lacking understanding, portrayed as burdensome: heavier than lead, sand, salt, or iron, hard to teach, and wearying through madness. His life is called worse than death, and he is mourned all his days. Chapter 22 closes by advising others not to talk with him, to beware, and to turn away; his fearful heart cannot withstand fear.

l: friend, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A friend is a relationship that survives a drawn sword or hostile words, allowing reconciliation, but ends through insult, arrogance, disclosed secrets, or treacherous blows, from which one flees. The speaker pledges to shelter a friend without shame, yet warns that evil coming through a friend makes others wary.

l: the dead, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The dead are people who deserve burial with due honor. They should be mourned with tears and lamentation, wrapped and buried without neglect; after a day or two sorrow should end, mindful of one's own death, and remembrance should rest too.

l: mourning, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: duration one day or two [according to the dead's merit] Mourning is to be bitter and passionate, according to the merit of the dead, but kept to one day or two so one is not spoken evil of. The text warns that sorrow brings death and saps strength, and the son is told not to give his heart to it, since it does the dead no good and harms the mourner.

l: friendship and reconciliation, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Friendship is fragile: insults dissolve it, as a stone scatters birds, and foreshadow bloodshed. Reconciliation remains possible after a drawn sword or harsh words, but not after insult, arrogance, betrayed secrets, or treachery. Loyalty in a neighbor's poverty earns shared prosperity.

l: speaker (author praying), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A speaker praying to the Lord as Father and Master of his life, asking not to be abandoned, for discipline over thought and heart, and for removal of pride, evil desire, gluttony, lust; then urges his children to learn mouth discipline.

l: Jacob, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Jacob is a patriarchal figure and people: Wisdom is told to dwell in him, Moses's law is an inheritance for his assemblies, and he receives blessing and covenant, with his inheritance divided among twelve tribes.

l: discipline of the mouth, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: effect_on_keeper not caught [for one who keeps it] The speaker teaches that whoever keeps the discipline of the mouth will not be caught, while the sinner, the insulter, and the arrogant stumble through their lips. It means avoiding habitual oaths, naming the Holy One, gross rudeness, and abusive language.

l: oaths, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A warning against habitual oath-taking: constantly uttering the Name leaves one unclean of sin, like a continually scourged servant with bruises. Many oaths fill a man with iniquity, and false swearing leaves him unjustified and his house full of calamities.

l: fornicator, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The fornicator is depicted as an insatiable man whose passion burns like fire; all bread tastes sweet to him, and he never stops until the fire burns out and he dies.

l: adulterous man, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: An adulterous man who strays from his marriage bed believes darkness and walls hide him and that the Most High forgets his sins. He fears human eyes, not the Lord's, and is finally punished, seized in the city streets unexpectedly.

l: adulterous wife, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A wife who leaves her husband and bears an heir by another man is charged with three offenses: disobeying the law of the Most High, wronging her husband, and committing adultery. She is brought out before the congregation, her punishment extends to her children, who take no root, and her cursed memory carries unblotted reproach.

l: Zion, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Zion is where Wisdom was established after she ministered before the Most High in the holy tabernacle.

l: Jerusalem, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Jerusalem is the beloved city and sanctuary city, the Lord's resting place. First it is where the Creator gave Wisdom rest and her domain; later a prayer asks compassion on it, to fill Zion with his glory.

l: book of the covenant, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The book of the covenant is the covenant of the Most High God, identified with all that Wisdom has said; it is the law Moses commanded as an inheritance for Jacob's assemblies.

l: Moses, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Moses is portrayed as a merciful man, loved by God and people. God glorified him before kings, sanctified him for faithfulness and meekness, spoke with him face to face, gave him the law to teach Israel, and he consecrated Aaron with holy oil.

l: wicked woman, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The wicked woman is portrayed in Chapter 25 as the worst malice, worse than any wound, calamity, or enemy's wrath; the speaker would prefer living with a lion and a dragon. She darkens her countenance like a bear, is blamed as the origin of sin and death, and is likened to a sandy hill for a quiet man. The speaker advises denying her freedom of speech and cutting her off from the husband's flesh.

l: husband (of the wicked woman), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The husband of the wicked woman is a figure in Chapter 25 who sits among neighbors sighing bitterly at his wife's conduct. A talkative or unhappy-making wife burdens him like a sandy hill for aged feet, leaving weak knees, a saddened face and wounded heart. He is advised not to be ensnared by beauty and to cut off a wife who will not follow his direction.

l: wisdom, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: is_beautiful_in elderly people Wisdom is called beautiful in old men, and the one who finds it is called great. Yet no one is greater than the one who fears the Lord.

l: elderly people, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The aged are portrayed as honored: their gray hair brings beautiful judgment, good counsel, wisdom, and experience as a crown, with fear of the Lord as glory. The records warn that those who gather nothing in youth find nothing in old age, and that an old adulterous fool is hated.

l: good wife, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The good wife is portrayed as a great gift given to those who fear the Lord and as her husband's richest treasure. Chapter 26 describes her bringing him joy and peace, delighting him with grace, and strengthening him with knowledge, while her silence, modesty, and self-control are prized and her beauty in an orderly home is likened to the rising sun. Chapter 36 calls her a help meet and pillar of support, whose cheering beauty and kind, humble speech set her husband apart.

l: husband, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A husband of a good wife is called happy: his days are doubled, he fulfills his years in peace, delights in her grace, and his bones are strengthened by her knowledge, unlike the man holding a wicked woman, likened to grasping a scorpion.

l: wicked woman, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A wicked woman, a negative figure in Chapter 26, is likened to a chafing yoke and a scorpion to whoever grasps her. The text condemns jealous, drunken, and fornicating women, ending with an image of her opening her mouth like a thirsty traveller drinking from any nearby water.

l: fear of the Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Fear of the Lord, in Chapter 40, is praised as better than riches and strength, lacking nothing and needing no outside help, and likened to a garden of blessing covering a person beyond any glory.

l: sin, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Sin, in Chapter 27, is pictured as a nail wedged between stones in buying and selling, then as a lion lurking for evildoers; many sin for profit, and wrath and anger are abominations sinners possess.

l: thoughts, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: is_test_of a person [compared to a furnace testing the potter's vessels] A person's thoughts are the test of the person, likened to a sieve that leaves refuse behind and a furnace that tests a potter's vessels. The utterance of the heart's thought discloses a person as fruit discloses a tree's cultivation, so no one should be praised before his thoughts are heard.

l: fools, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Fools are people whose discourse shifts like the moon, unlike the godly; their talk is offensive, laughter sinful, and swearing appalling, so the reader is finally advised to limit time among them.

l: one who reveals secrets, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A person who reveals secrets destroys trust and friendship with a neighbor, cannot find a close friend, and is likened to one releasing a bird or gazelle; unlike a wound or abuse, the damage leaves him hopeless.

l: friend, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The reader is told to love a friend and keep faith with him. A friend whose secrets are revealed goes far away and cannot be caught again, so the friendship is destroyed as an enemy is destroyed.

l: deceitful schemer, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A deceitful schemer who winks while plotting evil; he flatters sweetly in person, then twists words into traps afterward. Those who know him avoid him, and the Lord hates him.

l: evildoers, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Evildoers are warned that their own deeds will return upon them from an unknown source; like those who dig pits, cast stones, or set snares, they fall into their own traps, with sin lurking like a lion.

l: vengeance, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Vengeance is presented as self-defeating: whoever takes it will find vengeance from the Lord, and his sins will be made firm.

l: anger and wrath, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: is_nourished_by flesh [man as flesh] Anger and wrath are described as nourished by a man who is himself flesh, leaving no one to atone for his sins. The reader is told to stop enmity and not be angry with his neighbor, and a man's wrath is said to match his strength and wealth, like a fire matching its fuel.

l: forgiveness, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: leads_to pardon of sins [when one prays] Forgiving a neighbor the hurt he has done is the condition for having one's own sins pardoned when praying. The text asks how anyone can harbor anger and still expect healing from the Lord.

l: neighbor, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The neighbor is the person who may have done hurt and who should be forgiven. The reader is told not to be angry with him and to overlook ignorance.

l: vengeful man, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A vengeful man harbors anger, shows no mercy to others like himself, and cannot rightly seek forgiveness; consequently he receives the Lord's vengeance and his sins are made firm.

l: strife, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Strife is a kind of contention to abstain from, since abstaining diminishes sins; passionate men kindle it, and hasty quarrels spark fires and bloodshed, burning as fuel allows.

l: tongue, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The tongue is portrayed as a destructive force: a spark that burns or is quenched, its stroke breaks bones, and it kills more than the sword. Bound by iron and brass, it brings an evil death worse than Hades, falls on those forsaking the Lord, and the reader is urged to guard his mouth.

l: neighbor, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: receives loan [in time of his need] The neighbor is the one to whom a merciful person lends in time of need, and the lender is told to repay him on time and keep faith with him. He is also the person for whom a good man will be surety, and the reader is told to help him according to his power while taking care not to fall himself.

l: borrower (the one who receives a loan), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A borrower who treats a loan as a windfall: submissive, kissing the lender's hands until the money arrives. When repayment is due, he delays, makes excuses, blames the season, repays only half or with cursing and disgrace, and needlessly makes an enemy of the creditor.

l: creditor, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A creditor who lends to a needy neighbor acts mercifully and keeps the commandments, yet risks receiving hardly half back from an unfaithful borrower, or losing money and gaining an enemy. Fear of fraud deters many lenders, and creditors' insults grieve the understanding.

l: loan, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: is_considered_by_many windfall A loan is to be given to a neighbor in time of need and repaid on time. Many have treated loans as windfalls and caused trouble for those who helped them, and this fraud has led many to refuse to lend.

l: poor man, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A poor man who should receive help according to his need, with patience and no delay of alms, never sent away empty; his humble life in a log shelter is deemed better than feasting elsewhere.

l: guarantor, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A guarantor is a good man who stands surety for his neighbor and gives his life for him; the helped should remember this kindness, yet sinners waste the guarantor's property and the thankless abandon their deliverer.

l: suretyship, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Suretyship, discussed in Chapter 29, is portrayed as perilous: it has ruined prosperous people, shaking them like a sea wave and driving mighty men from their homes into foreign wandering, and it leads a sinner undertaking contracts into lawsuits.

l: foreign nations, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The foreign nations are to have the Lord's fear sent upon them and to see his mighty power raised against them. The prayer asks that they come to know that there is no God but him, and that he be magnified in them as he showed his holiness in his people.

l: sojourner, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A sojourner in Chapter 29 lives miserably, wandering from house to house and not daring to speak as a guest. He is told to set a table and feed his host, then ordered to leave when the host's brother, an honored guest, arrives.

l: host, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: gives bitter words [to the guest who entertains and serves, with no thanks] The host in this passage treats the sojourner harshly, ordering him to set the table and feed him from what is in his hand. He then dismisses the sojourner, saying that an honored guest has come and that he needs his house.

l: hospitality, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: is_grievous_to man of understanding [scolding about lodging and insults of creditors] Hospitality as depicted here is a burden for the dependent guest, who must entertain, serve drinks, and receive no thanks along with bitter words. The text prefers being content with little or much in one's own home, listing water, bread, a garment, and a house for privacy as life's essentials.

l: son, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The son is a figure whose outcome depends on upbringing: if chastised, given work, and kept from liberty in youth, he becomes his father's joy and likeness, avenging enemies and repaying friends' kindness; if unrestrained, he turns headstrong, stubborn, disobedient, shameless, like an unbroken horse.

l: father (the father of the son), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The father who loves his son lays stripes on him and thereby gains joy, profit, boasting among acquaintances, and rejoicing before friends. He dies as though not dead because he leaves behind a son like himself, and he dies without regret. One who makes too much of his son will bind up the boy's wounds and be troubled at every cry, and one who pampers or plays with him will be made afraid and grieved.

l: discipline and chastisement of children, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Child discipline is presented in Chapter 30 as strict chastisement: stripes, bowing the neck, beating in youth, and giving work. This prevents stubbornness and yields profit, joy, and honor for the father, whereas pampering and ignoring follies bring sorrow and a disobedient child.

l: health, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: is_better_than wealth Health is said to be better than all gold and wealth without measure; a poor man who is healthy and fit is better off than a rich man afflicted in body. Death and eternal rest are said to be better than a bitter life and continual sickness. Good things given to one who cannot enjoy them are compared to food offerings on a grave or before an idol.

l: sorrow, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Sorrow is a harmful emotion the reader is warned against: it has destroyed many and brings no profit, so one should not surrender to it and should remove it far away, like envy, wrath, and anxiety.

l: gladness and cheerfulness, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Gladness of heart is called a man's life and cheerfulness lengthens his days; no gladness exceeds heart's joy. The reader is urged to love his soul, comfort his heart, and eat cheerfully.

l: rich man (the rich person), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A rich man toils to gather money and, resting, is filled with his good things. If found blameless and not pursuing gold, he is called blessed for wonderful deeds; his prosperity is secured and the congregation proclaims his alms.

l: greed at table, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Greed at table is portrayed as a wicked thing, with the greedy eye called the most greedy creation. Guests at a great table are warned not to reach wherever the eye looks. The insatiable suffer wakefulness, colic and griping, and risk being hated and giving offense.

l: table manners and moderate eating, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Table manners and moderate eating, from Chapter 31, counsel consideration of neighbors, discretion, eating what is set before one, stopping first, and not reaching out before others. Little suffices the well-mannered; moderation brings healthy sleep, early rising and clear wits. Generosity earns blessings, stinginess earns the city's murmurs.

l: wine, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Wine is a substance whose value depends on how it is drunk. In season and moderation it is life-giving, created to gladden men with joy of heart and gladness of soul. Drunk excessively it brings bitterness, rage, conflict, weakened strength and wounds, destroying many and testing the proud's hearts like a furnace tests steel.

l: feast ruler, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The feast ruler is instructed not to exalt himself but to be one of the guests; he first attends to them before sitting, then, duties finished, is gladdened on their account and receives a wreath for good service.

l: older speaker, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: has_right_to speak [with sound knowledge, without interrupting the music] The older speaker is told it is his right to speak, but he must do so with sound knowledge. He must not interrupt the music.

l: young man, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: speaks no more than twice [only if asked] The young man is told to speak only if obliged, no more than twice, and only if asked. He should sum up his speech, saying many things in few words, like one who knows yet holds his tongue.

l: music, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Music is a topic in Chapter 32: it should not be interrupted by talk during performance, and concerts and melody are likened to ruby and emerald signets in gold at a pleasant wine banquet.

l: wine banquet, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The wine banquet is the setting where a music concert is compared to a ruby signet in gold, and musical melody with pleasant wine to an emerald signet in gold. Guests are told to rise in good time, go home quickly, amuse themselves, and avoid sinning by proud speech.

l: the law, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The law is trusted by the wise man of understanding and is faithful to him like a divine oracle, whereas a hypocrite about the law is unstable, like a boat in a storm.

l: men, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Men, like Adam, originate from the ground; the Lord holds them like clay in a potter's hand, blessing some and cursing others, making their ways different.

l: opposites in pairs, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Chapter 33 presents a theme of paired opposites: good against evil, life against death, sinner against godly. It concludes that all works of the Most High come in contrasting pairs, one against another.

l: slave owner, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A slave owner is instructed to assign his slave fitting work for discipline, rest and preventing idleness, avoiding excess or injustice, and to treat him like himself, since he was bought with blood and is needed like one's own soul.

l: potter, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A potter, anxiously busy at his wheel, produces handiwork in quantity: he shapes clay with his arm, turns the wheel with his feet, carefully finishes the glazing, and cleans the kiln.

l: dreams, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Dreams are portrayed as vain things and reflections that give wings to fools and lead many astray; likened to grasping shadows or chasing wind, the reader is warned not to trust them unless sent by the Most High.

l: wrongful sacrifices, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Wrongful sacrifices are offerings made from ill-gotten goods. They are declared a mockery, unacceptable to the Lord, and unable to pacify sins however numerous. The text escalates: sacrificing from the poor's goods equals killing a son before his father, and depriving the needy of bread or wages is murder.

l: wisdom, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: is_complete_in faithful mouth The wise man seeks out the wisdom of the ancients, and through the spirit of understanding he pours forth the words of his wisdom. Nations will declare his wisdom, and the congregation will proclaim his praise.

l: righteous man, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: has_sacrifice_that_is acceptable [will not be forgotten] The righteous man's sacrifice is described as acceptable and unforgotten, and his offering enriches the altar with a sweet fragrance before the Most High. Those who serve God according to his good pleasure are accepted, and the prayer of the humble pierces the clouds.

l: offerings and sacrifices, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Offerings and sacrifices are commanded and likened to obedience, kindness, alms-giving, and avoiding wickedness. The righteous offering enriches the altar and smells sweet before the Most High. Readers should not come empty, should give first fruits and tithes cheerfully, and never offer unrighteous bribes.

l: fatherless and widow, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: has_cry_against unmerciful and unrighteous [the one who caused the widow's tears] The Lord will in no way despise the supplication of the fatherless or the widow when she pours out her tale. The widow's tears running down her cheek are said to be a cry against the one who caused them to fall.

l: unmerciful and unrighteous, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The unmerciful will have their loins crushed, and the arrogant multitude will be taken away and the sceptres of the unrighteous broken in pieces. The Lord will repay them with vengeance and will not be patient toward them. Gifts and unrighteous sacrifices will not win his acceptance.

l: divine judgment, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The Lord's impartial, righteous judgment renders to everyone according to deeds and plans; it unfolds as vengeance on the heathen, arrogant, and unrighteous, ending in rejoicing and mercy for his people.

l: Aaron, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Aaron is Moses' brother from the tribe of Levi, exalted as a holy man and given the priesthood by an everlasting covenant. Dressed in glorious garments and anointed by Moses, he is chosen from all the living to offer sacrifice, incense and atonement, teach Israel the law, and bless the people. Strangers envied him in the wilderness, but God destroyed them and added glory to him. He receives first fruits but no land, since the Lord is his portion.

l: adversary and enemy, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: has_rulers_who_say There is no one but ourselves [rulers of the enemies] The adversary and enemy are to be taken away and destroyed, with indignation and wrath poured out on them. Those who escape are to be devoured by raging fire, those who harm the Lord's people are to find destruction, and the enemy rulers who say "There is no one but ourselves" are to have their heads crushed.

l: husband, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: is_unlike_other_men wife with kind and humble tongue [if kindness and humility are on her tongue] A husband who has a wife gets his richest treasure, help, and support, and is unlike other men if his wife speaks with kindness and humility. A man with no wife is compared to unfenced property that is plundered and to a wanderer who mourns and lodges wherever nightfall finds him, and who is not trusted.

l: friend, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A friend, as described in Chapter 37, may be one in name only: rejoicing in good times, then turning against a person in affliction or fleeing in battle. Such a friend turned enemy brings grief to death; a true friend should be remembered, even in riches.

l: counselor, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A counselor figure, warned against in Chapter 37: all praise counsel, but some advise for their own interest, so beware, learn his interest beforehand, since he may approve your way then watch the outcome.

l: counsel, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Counsel is a topic of advice praised by every counselor and meant to precede every action. Chapter 37 warns against seeking it from the jealous or biased, upholds one's own heart's counsel as most faithful, and urges asking the Most High to direct one's way.

l: godly man, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The godly man keeps the commandments and is the one to stay continually with; in Chapter 37 he is described as sharing the reader's own soul and grieving with the reader if he fails.

l: wise man, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A wise man who instructs his own people, whose understanding bears trustworthy fruit. He is blessed, called happy by all who see him, inherits confidence among his people, and his name lives forever, unlike the clever instructor unprofitable to his own soul.

l: gluttony, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Gluttony is insatiable greed in luxury and eating, warned against in Chapter 37: it causes nausea, disease and many deaths, while heeding the warning prolongs life.

l: medicines, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Medicines are created by the Lord from the earth, and a prudent man will not despise them. Physicians use them to heal and ease pain, pharmacists mix them, and water made sweet with wood illustrates their power.

l: sick person (the son addressed), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A sick person, addressed as son, is counseled in Chapter 38 to pray to the Lord, put away wrongdoing, cleanse his heart, offer fine flour and oil, then give the needed physician a place.

l: plowman, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A plowman who drives oxen, holds the plow, glories in the goad and talks of bulls; the text doubts his wisdom, as he fixes on turning furrows and loses sleep feeding heifers.

l: craftsman, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The craftsman is a diligent, skillful worker who labors night and day, striving for variety and faithful likeness in finished work. Though sustaining cities and the age through craft-as-prayer, he is absent from the people's council, valued for his hands rather than public counsel.

l: smith, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A smith who sits by the anvil working unwrought iron; despite smoke, heat and deafening hammer noise wearing his body, he keeps his eyes on the pattern, devoted to perfecting and adorning his works.

l: wise man (he who meditates in the law), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The wise man is one who meditates in the law of the Most High, applying his soul to it and glorying in the covenant of the Lord. He seeks the wisdom of the ancients, serves among great men, and travels foreign nations, learning good and evil. He prays early and asks pardon; if the Lord wills, he pours forth wisdom. Nations and the congregation praise him, and his name endures across generations.

l: holy children, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: are_addressed_by speaker The speaker, who is filled like the full moon, tells the holy children to listen and to bud forth like a rose by a brook. They are urged to give a sweet fragrance like frankincense, flower like a lily, sing a song of praise and bless the Lord for all his works. They are also given words to say in praise.

l: sinners and the wicked, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: receive evil things [created from the beginning for sinners] The Lord's ways are plain to the holy but stumbling blocks to the wicked. Evil things were created from the beginning for sinners, and life's necessities turn into evils for them. The ungodly are punished to destruction by the sword and other instruments of vengeance.

l: instruments of vengeance, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Instruments of vengeance are winds, fire, hail, famine, death, wild beasts, scorpions, adders and the sword, created by their maker for punishment. They strike in fury at the time of reckoning, appeasing his wrath, rejoicing in his commandment and never disobeying it in season.

l: necessities of life, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Necessities of life, listed in Chapter 39 as water, fire, iron, salt, wheat flour, honey, milk, grape blood, oil and clothing, are good for the godly but become evils for sinners.

l: praise and prayer, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: is_directed_to the Lord [holy children told to bless him with songs and harps] The wise man rises early to make supplication before the Most High, opens his mouth in prayer, asks pardon for his sins, and gives thanks to the Lord. The holy children are told to magnify the Lord's name with songs and harps and to say that all his works are exceedingly good. The chapter ends by calling all to sing praises with their whole hearts and voices and bless the Lord's name.

l: human travail and troubled sleep, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Human travail and troubled sleep: great travail is created for every man, with fear of death afflicting all from throne to burlap. Even in bed, night sleep brings wrath, fear and visions; he rests little, wakes marveling the fear is nothing.

l: things better than both, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A series of comparisons in Chapter 40 sets one good thing above two others: wisdom's love beats wine and music, a blameless wife beats children and a city. It extends to treasure, tongue, almsgiving, counsel, and fear of the Lord.

l: begging, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Begging is condemned as worse than death. A son is warned in Chapter 40 not to live as a beggar: one who depends on another's table has no life worth considering, pollutes his soul, and begging burns his belly though sweet to the shameless.

l: sinners and the ungodly, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Sinners and the ungodly forsook the law of the Most High God; cursed at birth and in death, they travel from curse to perdition, their evil name blotted out and their children disgraced.

l: children of sinners, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Children of sinners are deemed abominable and dwell among the ungodly; their inheritance perishes and their posterity bears perpetual disgrace, so they complain against their ungodly father for the shame suffered on his account.

l: good name, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A good name is urged as worth regarding because it outlasts a thousand great treasures of gold; a good life has limited days, but a good name continues forever.

l: shame, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Shame is treated as a moral topic in Chapter 41: it is fitting only for particular wrongs, not everything. Listed examples include sexual immorality before parents, lying before a prince, offense before a judge, iniquity before the congregation, unjust dealing with partner or friend, theft, and revealing secrets. Being ashamed of the right things earns favor in everyone's sight, while retaining every kind of shame is not good.

l: daughter (a father's daughter), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: is_cause_of wakefulness to her father [secret cause] A daughter is described as a secret cause of her father's wakefulness, with worries about her youth, marriage, virginity, faithfulness and barrenness. A headstrong daughter is to be watched strictly lest she make her father a laughingstock and shame him in public.

l: honest business dealings, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Guidance on honest business dealings: don't be ashamed of exact scales and weights, fair reckoning with partners and travellers, or bargaining with merchants; hand over goods by number and weight, and record all giving and receiving in writing.

l: the sun, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The sun is a marvelous instrument made by the Lord, which gives light and looks at all things. It rises bringing tidings, then at noon burns three times hotter than a furnace, drying the land and blinding eyes, its course hastened at the Lord's word.

l: Jacob's people, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Jacob's people are a community of Israel whose story is told across the records. Despite wonders by Elijah and Elisha, they stayed unrepentant and were carried off as plunder and scattered, leaving few under a ruler from David's house, some righteous and some sinful. When Sennacherib's boasting shook them, they prayed and were delivered. Later they gather around Simon, worship, receive his blessing, and the author prays for Israel's joy and peace forever.

l: moon, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The moon is a celestial object marking seasons, declaring times, and serving as a sign for the world and feast days; it names the month, wanes upon completing its course, and wonderfully increases as an instrument of the army on high.

l: snow, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Snow is made to fall by the Lord's commandment, sprinkled down like flying birds and like descending locusts; its dazzling whiteness amazes the eye and the heart as it falls.

l: sea, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The sea is a body of water the Lord calmed by his counsel and planted with islands; sailors recount its dangers, and it holds strange, wondrous works: varied living things and huge creatures.

l: sky, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: has_attribute clear [pride of the heavenly heights] The clear sky is called the pride of the heavenly heights and the appearance of heaven in the spectacle of its glory. The rainbow encircles it with a glorious circle stretched out by the hands of the Most High, and the stars shine in its highest places.

l: famous men, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Famous men are ancestors praised across generations, endowed by the Lord with great glory as rulers, counselors, prophets and composers. Those of mercy, whose righteous deeds endure, leave a lasting name, inheritance for offspring, and peaceful burial.

l: Enoch, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Enoch pleased the Lord, was taken up from earth unlike any created man, and stands as an example of repentance to all generations.

l: Noah, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Noah is a perfect, righteous man who, in the season of wrath, kept the race alive so a remnant survived the flood, and then received everlasting covenants that flesh would never again be destroyed by flood.

l: Abraham, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Abraham is portrayed as a great father of a multitude of nations, unmatched in glory. He kept the Most High's law, bore the covenant in his flesh, and proved faithful when tested, so he received an oath of blessing for nations, countless offspring, and inheritance.

l: Isaac, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: receives covenant [same assurance, for Abraham's sake] God established the same assurance in Isaac for the sake of his father Abraham. This included the blessing of all men and the covenant.

l: covenant, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The covenant is the lasting bond within which the righteous men's children remain. It was made everlasting with Noah against another flood, established in Abraham's flesh, and passed through Isaac to Jacob and the twelve tribes.

l: priesthood (Aaron's priesthood), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: has_duration everlasting [to Aaron and his offspring] The priesthood was given to Aaron by an everlasting covenant, to him and his offspring, to minister to the Lord, offer sacrifices twice daily, burn incense, make atonement, and bless the people in his name. No stranger may wear its garments, only his sons and offspring perpetually. Its holders receive first fruits and sacrifices but no land inheritance, and the dignity of the priesthood is confirmed to Phinehas and his offspring forever.

l: priestly garments (Aaron's garments), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Aaron's priestly garments comprise linen trousers, a long robe, the ephod, and a gold, blue, purple and scarlet holy garment, with pomegranates and golden bells, Urim and Thummim, engraved tribal stones set in gold, and a gold mitre crown engraved "HOLINESS". Unprecedented in kind, they are worn perpetually only by Aaron's sons and offspring; the bells remind the people.

l: sons of Aaron, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: is_a priests [hold the Lord's offering before Israel] The sons of Aaron stood in their glory holding the Lord's offering before all the congregation of Israel. After Simon poured the libation, they shouted and sounded the trumpets of beaten work with a great fanfare as a reminder before the Most High.

l: Phinehas, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Phinehas, son of Eleazar, is honored as third in glory for zeal in the fear of the Lord. He stood fast when the people turned away and atoned for Israel, so a covenant of peace made him leader of the sanctuary, with priesthood forever for his offspring.

l: David, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: David, son of Jesse of the tribe of Judah, is praised as a figure set apart from Israel like fat from the peace offering. In youth he killed Goliath with a sling stone after calling on the Lord, and defeated the Philistines. He loved the Lord, set singers before the altar, and ordered feasts and seasons. The Lord gave him a covenant of kings, a glorious throne in Israel, a wise son Solomon, and a root from his family.

l: covenant, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The chapter names several covenants: God's teaching of Jacob the covenant through Moses, the everlasting covenant of priesthood with Aaron and his offspring, and the covenant of peace with Phinehas. God also made a covenant with David the son of Jesse of the tribe of Judah, whose kingly inheritance passes from son to son, paralleled with Aaron's inheritance passing to his seed.

l: house for God's name (Solomon's temple), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The temple was repaired and strengthened by Simon, with its foundation built to the height of the double walls, the lofty retaining walls of the enclosure. A water cistern like the sea in circumference was dug in his days. Its court was made glorious when Simon ascended the holy altar in his robe.

l: Joshua the son of Nun, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Joshua son of Nun was a valiant warrior who succeeded Moses in prophecies. Made great to save God's elect and give Israel their inheritance, he took vengeance on enemies. He raised his sword against cities, saw the sun go back by his hand, and called on the Most High, who sent hailstones. With Caleb he withstood the adversary in Moses' time, one of only two preserved to enter the land.

l: Caleb the son of Jephunneh, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Caleb, son of Jephunneh, stood with Joshua against the adversary and stilled the people's wicked complaining under Moses. One of only two preserved of six hundred thousand, he received lasting strength from the Lord into old age, entered the hill country, and his offspring inherited it.

l: Samuel, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Samuel is a prophet of the Lord, loved by him. He established a kingdom, anointed princes over the people, and judged the congregation by the Lord's law. His faithfulness proved him a prophet. He called on the Lord with a suckling lamb offering when enemies pressed. Before death he testified he had taken no one's goods, and no one accused him; after falling asleep he prophesied and showed the king his end.

l: the judges, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: has_disposition faithful to the Lord [hearts not engaged in immorality, did not turn away] The judges are blessed, each by name, as those whose hearts did not engage in immorality or turn away from the Lord. The text prays that their memory be blessed, their bones flourish again out of their place, and their names be renewed in their children.

l: Solomon, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Solomon, David's wise son, reigns in peace as God gives him rest on every side. He builds a house for God's name, becomes famed for wisdom, proverbs and songs, and amasses gold and silver like common metals. Yet he bows to women, blemishing his honor and defiling his offspring, then dies, leaving Rehoboam.

l: Rehoboam, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: is_a one who lacked understanding [foolishness of the people] Rehoboam is named as Solomon's offspring, described as the foolishness of the people and one who lacked understanding. By his counsel he made the people revolt.

l: Jeroboam the son of Nebat, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Jeroboam son of Nebat is a figure said to have made Israel sin, and he gave Ephraim a way of sin.

l: Ephraim, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A disobedient kingdom ruled out of Ephraim after the sovereignty was divided. Jeroboam the son of Nebat gave Ephraim a way of sin.

l: kingdom's division (Israel's sovereignty), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: results_in Ephraim [disobedient kingdom ruled out of Ephraim] The sovereignty was divided because of Solomon's folly, and a disobedient kingdom ruled out of Ephraim. Rehoboam's counsel made the people revolt, and Jeroboam son of Nebat led Israel into sin. Even so, the Lord left a remnant to Jacob and a root to David.

l: Israel's sins and removal from the land, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Jeroboam gave Ephraim a way of sin; the people's sins multiplied exceedingly and they sought all manner of wickedness, until vengeance came and they were removed from their land.

l: Solomon's women and folly, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: causes kingdom's division (Israel's sovereignty) [blemished honor, defiled offspring] Solomon bowed his loins to women and in his body was brought into subjection. This blemished his honor, defiled his offspring, and brought wrath upon his children, which grieved the speaker, and the kingdom was divided as a result.

l: Elijah, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Elijah is praised as a prophet whose word burned like a torch. By his zeal he brought famine, raised a dead man by the word of the Most High, and brought down kings. He heard rebuke at Sinai and judgments at Horeb, and anointed kings for retribution. He was taken up in a tempest of fire in a fiery chariot, leaving Elisha filled with his spirit. He was recorded as a reprover to pacify anger and restore Jacob's tribes.

l: Elisha, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Elisha is a figure filled with Elijah's spirit when Elijah was taken in a whirlwind; fearless before rulers and subject to no one, nothing was too hard for him, and his buried body prophesied, so his works were marvelous in death.

l: Hezekiah, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Hezekiah, a king of David's line, fortified his city and built water works, tunneling through rock and making cisterns. When Sennacherib invaded, he and his people called on the Lord and were delivered. He pleased the Lord, followed David's ways, and in his days the sun went backward and his life was prolonged.

l: Isaiah, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Isaiah is a great and faithful prophet who, by an excellent spirit, foresaw the future. The Lord delivered the people from Sennacherib's invasion by his hand. He commanded the ways of David that Hezekiah followed, comforted mourners in Zion, and revealed hidden things and events to the end of time. In his days the sun went backward and the king's life was prolonged.

l: Sennacherib, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Sennacherib, an arrogant Assyrian invader in Hezekiah's days, sent Rabshakeh against Jerusalem, boasted against Zion and frightened the people, then departed after the Lord's angel utterly destroyed his camp.

l: Assyrian invasion of Jerusalem, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: ended_with Assyrians [camp struck, utterly destroyed by the Lord's angel] In Hezekiah's days Sennacherib invaded and sent Rabshakeh, and then departed, having lifted his hand against Zion and boasted in arrogance. The people were shaken and in pain like women in labor, and called on the Lord. The Holy One heard them from Heaven and delivered them by the hand of Isaiah, as the Lord's angel struck and utterly destroyed the camp of the Assyrians.

l: Josiah, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Josiah is a king whose memory is likened to sweet incense, honey and banquet music. He reformed the people, removed abominations, set his heart right toward the Lord, and made godliness prevail in lawless days, ranking with David and Hezekiah as non-wicked kings.

l: kings of Judah, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The kings of Judah were, except David, Hezekiah, and Josiah, wicked for abandoning the Most High's law; consequently the kingship ended, with their power given to others and glory to a foreign nation.

l: Jeremiah, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Jeremiah, sanctified in the womb as a prophet, was mistreated by Judah's kings yet wrote of the chosen city's burning and desolation, appointed to uproot, destroy, build, and plant.

l: Ezekiel, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: saw vision of glory [shown by God] Ezekiel saw the vision of glory that God showed him on the chariot of the cherubim. He is also said to have remembered the enemies in rainstorm and to have done good to those who directed their ways aright.

l: twelve prophets, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: comforted Jacob's people [delivered them by confident hope] The twelve prophets are blessed with the wish that their bones flourish again out of their place. They comforted the people of Jacob and delivered them by confident hope.

l: Zerubbabel, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: is_like signet ring [on the right hand] Zerubbabel is asked about in the phrase 'How shall we magnify' him, and is likened to a signet ring on the right hand.

l: Jesus the son of Josedek, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Jesus the son of Josedek, in Zerubbabel's days, built the house and exalted a holy people to the Lord, prepared for everlasting glory.

l: Nehemiah, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Nehemiah, a man of great memory, rebuilt: he raised fallen walls, set up gates and bars, and restored the people's houses.

l: Simon, the son of Onias, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Simon, son of Onias, is a high priest who repaired the house, strengthened the temple, dug a cistern, and fortified the city against siege to save his people from ruin. The records close by praising his splendor as he leads the altar service, pours the libation, and blesses the congregation.

l: temple worship service (Simon's liturgy), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Simon finishes the service at the altars, receives the portions from the priests' hands, and pours the cup of the grape at the foot of the altar. The sons of Aaron then sound trumpets, the people fall in worship, the singers sing, and the people pray until the service is finished. Simon then goes down, lifts his hands over the congregation, and bows a second time to declare the blessing from the Most High.

l: Jesus, the son of Sirach Eleazar, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Jesus, son of Sirach Eleazar of Jerusalem, identifies himself as author of the book of instruction, pouring wisdom from his heart, and closes by lamenting two nations that vex him and a third that is no nation.

l: book of instruction (Jesus's book), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: contains instruction of understanding and knowledge The book is described as containing the instruction of understanding and knowledge, written by Jesus, the son of Sirach Eleazar. Whoever exercises these things and lays them up in his heart will become wise. One who does them will be strong in all things, with the light of the Lord as his guide.

l: speaker (narrator of Chapter 51), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The narrator of Chapter 51 thanks the Lord for rescuing him from death, enemies, and a slanderous tongue before the king, after finding no human help. He recounts seeking wisdom from youth, praying at the temple, gaining a good possession and rest, and invites the uneducated to learn.

l: wisdom, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Wisdom, spoken of as 'her', is a gift from the Lord. The speaker sought her in prayer from youth, found her in purity, and gained instruction and rest. She is near, obtainable without money, and worth more than silver and gold.

l: slanderous tongue, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A slanderous, unclean, unrighteous tongue with lying words slandered the speaker to the king; the Lord delivered him from it near death, then gave him a tongue as reward to praise him.

l: uneducated (those invited to learn), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The uneducated are a group invited by the speaker to live in the house of instruction. Thirsty in soul and lacking wisdom, they are urged to get wisdom without money, take her yoke, receive instruction, rejoice in the Lord's mercy, and work before the time comes.

l: affliction (speaker's deliverance from death), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: is_a many afflictions endured by the speaker [from which the Lord delivered him] The speaker endured many afflictions: teeth ready to devour, fire on every side, and surrounding enemies, until his soul drew near to death and his life near to Hades. With no human help, he prayed from the earth and called on the Lord not to forsake him in the days of affliction. He was heard, saved from destruction and delivered from the evil time.

l: Daniel (Greek)
s: This is the Book of Daniel in its longer form with the Greek portions, in fourteen chapters. It follows Daniel, a Jewish youth taken into Babylonian service, and his companions Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, renamed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. The central theme is that the God of Israel rules over kings and kingdoms, and that faithful servants are vindicated. Chapters 1 to 6 are court tales. After Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem, the four youths are trained in Babylon. Daniel refuses the king's food, and God gives them wisdom. Daniel then recovers and interprets Nebuchadnezzar's forgotten dream of a great image, and is promoted. Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego refuse to worship a golden image and are thrown into a furnace. An angel protects them, Azarias prays, the three sing a hymn, and the king honors their God. Nebuchadnezzar's dream of a tree leads to his seven-times madness and restoration after he acknowledges the Most High. At Belshazzar's feast, using the temple vessels, a hand writes on the wall. Daniel reads it as the end of Belshazzar's kingdom, and Belshazzar is slain, with Darius the Mede receiving the kingdom. Under Darius, jealous officials trap Daniel with a decree against petition, and he is cast into the lions' den. An angel shuts the lions' mouths, and his accusers are destroyed instead. Chapters 7 to 12 are visions. Daniel sees four beasts, the Ancient of Days, and one like a son of man given everlasting dominion, with the saints of the Most High receiving the kingdom. A ram and goat vision, explained by Gabriel, concerns Media, Persia, Greece, and a fierce-faced king who desecrates the sanctuary. Daniel prays a confession for Jerusalem, and Gabriel announces seventy weeks. A radiant man in linen strengthens Daniel, speaks of conflict with the princes of Persia and Greece, and names Michael as Daniel's prince. Chapter 11 details wars between the kings of the south and north and a self-exalting king. Chapter 12 promises Michael's arising, deliverance for those written in the book, resurrection to life or shame, sealed words, and day counts of 1,290 and 1,335, with Daniel told he will stand in his inheritance at the end of the days. Chapters 13 and 14 add two stories. In Susanna, two lustful elders falsely accuse her, and Daniel exposes them by questioning them separately about the tree. In Bel and the Dragon, under Cyrus, Daniel shows through ashes that the priests, not the idol Bel, eat the offerings, destroys Bel and the dragon, and survives a second lions' den, fed by Habakkuk, before his accusers are devoured.

l: Daniel, Daniel (Greek)
s: Daniel is a Jewish youth of the captivity of Judah, taken to Babylon and renamed Belteshazzar. He is a faithful worshipper of the living God of heaven, who gives him understanding in all visions and dreams. The records open with him refusing the king's delicacies and wine to avoid defiling himself, proposing a ten-day test, and being found ten times better than the magicians and enchanters with his companions Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. He serves until the first year of Cyrus. Under Nebuchadnezzar he reveals and interprets the king's secret dream, crediting God rather than his own wisdom, and is rewarded with rule over Babylon's province and chief governorship over the wise men, while securing posts for Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. He later interprets the tree dream and counsels the king to break off his sins by righteousness and mercy to the poor. Under Belshazzar, recommended by the queen as having the spirit of the holy gods, he declines rewards, rebukes the king's pride, reads MENE, TEKEL, and PERES, and is proclaimed third ruler. Under Darius he is one of three presidents, distinguished by an excellent spirit and faithfulness; he keeps praying three times a day toward Jerusalem despite the decree, is cast into the lions' den, and is found unharmed because he trusted his God. He prospers under Darius and Cyrus the Persian. The second half centres on his own dreams and visions: the four animals and the horn in Belshazzar's first year; the vision at Susa by the Ulai in the third year, in which Gabriel frightens and then raises him; his understanding of Jeremiah's seventy years and his prayer of confession for himself and his people; and the great vision by the Hiddekel of a man clothed in linen. Gabriel and the man in linen call him greatly beloved. He is commanded to seal the book until the time of the end, and is promised that he will rest and stand in his inheritance at the end of the days. Additional episodes show him as a young youth raised up by God's holy spirit to rescue Susanna by exposing the elders' false testimony, gaining great reputation. Living with the king and honored above his friends, he refuses to worship Bel, destroys Bel and the dragon, is thrown into the lions' den again, is fed through Habakkuk, and is found alive on the seventh day and drawn out by the king.

l: Hananiah, Daniel (Greek)
s: Hananiah, a child of Judah renamed Shadrach by the prince of the eunuchs, joins Daniel in the vegetable-and-water diet test, receives knowledge and skill from God, is found unequaled by the king, and serves Nebuchadnezzar.

l: Mishael, Daniel (Greek)
s: Mishael, a child of Judah renamed Meshach by the prince of the eunuchs, joins Daniel in the ten-day vegetable and water test, receives knowledge and skill from God, and serves Nebuchadnezzar after proving unequaled.

l: Azariah, Daniel (Greek)
s: Azariah, a child of Judah, is renamed Abednego by the prince of the eunuchs, joins Daniel in the ten-day test, receives knowledge and skill from God, and serves the king, who finds no one like him.

l: Nebuchadnezzar, Daniel (Greek)
s: Nebuchadnezzar is the king of Babylon, called king of kings, represented in the great image as the head of gold, and father of Belshazzar. He besieged Jerusalem, took golden and silver vessels from the temple there, and had Israelite youths trained at his table, finding them ten times better than his magicians and enchanters. Troubled by a dream he could not remember, he threatened his wise men with death until Daniel revealed and interpreted it. He then worshipped Daniel, called Daniel's God the God of gods and Lord of kings, and made Daniel ruler over the province of Babylon. He later set up a golden image on the plain of Dura and decreed worship of it on pain of the fiery furnace. Enraged by Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, he had them cast in, saw four men walking unharmed, blessed their God, and promoted the three. After boasting of the Babylon he built as his royal dwelling, he was driven from men, ate grass like oxen, and lived like the animals until his understanding returned. Restored, he worshipped and praised the Most High God, who had given him kingdom, greatness, glory, and majesty, and declared that God humbles the proud.

l: Ashpenaz, Daniel (Greek)
s: is_a master of the eunuchs [of Nebuchadnezzar] Ashpenaz, master of the king's eunuchs, was commanded by the king to bring in Israelite youths of royal and noble descent who were without defect and skilled in wisdom, and to teach them the Chaldeans' learning and language. The text identifies the prince of the eunuchs, who renamed the four youths, favored Daniel, and brought them before the king, but does not explicitly say this is Ashpenaz.

l: Most High God, Daniel (Greek)
s: Most High God is the everlasting, living God of heaven who creates the sky and the earth and holds sovereignty over all flesh. Across the records he is a revealer of secrets, possessing wisdom and might, controlling times and seasons, and removing and setting up kings. His kingdom is indestructible and his dominion everlasting, and his power is unstoppable: no one can stay his hand or ask what he is doing. He is also righteous in all his works, keeps covenant and loving kindness with those who love him and keep his commandments, and holds mercies and forgiveness. He brought his people out of Egypt with a mighty hand and holds Jerusalem as his city and holy mountain. The account unfolds through a series of episodes. In the opening, he gives Jehoiakim into Nebuchadnezzar's hand and grants Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom, with Daniel understanding visions and dreams. He then reveals the king's dream to Daniel in answer to prayer, and Nebuchadnezzar acknowledges him as God of gods and Lord of kings. When the three men refuse the image, he sends his angel to save them from the furnace, and Nebuchadnezzar declares that no other god can deliver like this. He gives Nebuchadnezzar a kingdom, works signs and wonders toward him, and humbles him until the king acknowledges that God rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whomever he will. Belshazzar, who lifted himself up and did not glorify the God who holds his breath and ways, loses his kingdom to the Medes and Persians. Daniel's God then shuts the lions' mouths, and Darius declares him the living God, steadfast forever, who delivers and works signs and wonders. Later passages look forward: the Most High is the one against whom a final king speaks, while his saints receive and possess the kingdom forever. In prayer he is addressed as great and dreadful, righteous, merciful and forgiving, who confirmed the curse written in the law of Moses.
