The closing episodes show him hearing Susanna's cry and raising up Daniel to save her, and sending dinner to Daniel in the lions' den, leading the king to praise him as the God beside whom there is none other.

l: Jerusalem, Daniel (Greek)
s: Jerusalem is God's city, called by his name, lying desolate seventy years and a reproach to its neighbors because of inherited sins. Daniel pleads for mercy; Gabriel foretells rebuilding in troubled times, then destruction of city and sanctuary with determined desolations.

l: Israel, Daniel (Greek)
s: Israel is a people called by God's name who, having transgressed his law and disobeyed the prophets, now lie under the curse and oath of Moses' law, scattered through the countries where God drove them, bearing confusion of face.

l: Chaldeans, Daniel (Greek)
s: The Chaldeans are Babylonian wise men, counted among magicians, enchanters and sorcerers, who serve the king. In Chapter 2 they address him in Syrian, ask to hear the dream, and declare only the gods can reveal it, provoking his decree to destroy all wise men. In Chapter 5 they are summoned with rewards offered but cannot read the writing.

l: youths (selected Israelite captives), Daniel (Greek)
s: Selected Israelite youths of royal and noble families, chosen for flawlessness, good looks, wisdom, and palace ability. The king ordered them taught Chaldean learning and language and nourished three years before serving him. Four from Judah, eating vegetables, looked better than those eating the king's delicacies.

l: king's delicacies and wine, Daniel (Greek)
s: The king appointed a daily portion of his delicacies and the wine he drank for the selected youths for three years. Daniel purposed not to defile himself with them, and the youths who ate them looked less fair and less fat than the four after ten days. The steward then took away the delicacies and wine of the four.

l: vegetables and water diet, Daniel (Greek)
s: results_in fairer faces and fatter flesh [compared with youths who ate the king's delicacies] Daniel proposed that he and his three companions be given vegetables to eat and water to drink instead of the king's food. After the test, the four appeared fairer and fatter than those who ate the king's delicacies, so the steward kept them on vegetables.

l: golden and silver vessels (from the Jerusalem temple), Daniel (Greek)
s: originates_from temple in Jerusalem [taken by Nebuchadnezzar] These vessels were taken by Nebuchadnezzar from the temple in Jerusalem. Belshazzar commands that they be brought so that he, his lords, wives, and concubines can drink from them, which Daniel later cites as an offense against the Lord of heaven.

l: ten-day test, Daniel (Greek)
s: has_duration ten days Daniel asked the steward to test the four youths for ten days on vegetables and water and then compare their faces with those of the youths eating the king's delicacies. The steward agreed, and at the end of ten days the four looked fairer and fatter, which led him to remove their delicacies and wine permanently.

l: wise men of Babylon, Daniel (Greek)
s: is_chief_governed_by Daniel The wise men of Babylon, including magicians, enchanters, sorcerers, and Chaldeans, cannot tell the king his forgotten dream. The king decrees they be slain, and Arioch goes out to kill them. Daniel's revelation spares them, and Daniel is later made chief governor over them.

l: Nebuchadnezzar's dream, Daniel (Greek)
s: Nebuchadnezzar's troubling dream, forgotten by the king, is revealed to Daniel in a night vision: a great image struck and destroyed by a stone that becomes a mountain filling the earth; Daniel declares it certain.

l: great image, Daniel (Greek)
s: A mighty, bright, terrifying great image with a head of fine gold, silver chest and arms, bronze belly and thighs, iron legs, and feet of part iron, part clay. A stone cut without hands strikes the feet, shattering it into chaff the wind carries away, leaving no trace.

l: stone, Daniel (Greek)
s: A stone cut from the mountain without hands strikes the image's iron-and-clay feet, shattering it, then grows into a great mountain filling the earth; Daniel interprets it as God's kingdom.

l: interpretation of the dream, Daniel (Greek)
s: is_revealed_by God of heaven [to Daniel in a night vision] Daniel tells the king he is the head of gold, followed by an inferior kingdom, a third of bronze ruling all the earth, and a fourth strong as iron that crushes all things. The fourth kingdom becomes divided, part iron and part clay, partly strong and partly brittle, with peoples mingling but not clinging together. In the days of those kings God will set up a kingdom that destroys all the others and stands forever.

l: four kingdoms, Daniel (Greek)
s: Chapter 2 describes four successive kingdoms symbolized by an image's metals: Nebuchadnezzar's head of gold, an inferior second, a bronze third ruling all the earth, and a fourth strong as iron, crushing everything, which finally becomes divided, partly strong and partly brittle, with iron mixed with clay.

l: everlasting kingdom, Daniel (Greek)
s: The everlasting kingdom is a kingdom that endures forever, never destroyed or left to another people. In Chapter 2, Daniel says the God of heaven will set it up, and it will break in pieces and consume the other kingdoms, pictured by a stone becoming a mountain filling the earth. In Chapter 7, it is given to the one like a son of man and the saints, and all dominions serve him.

l: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, Daniel (Greek)
s: Three Jews holding appointed positions in Babylon who serve the God of Israel. Accused of refusing the king's gods and the golden image, they declared God could deliver them, yet would refuse regardless. Thrown into the furnace, they walked unharmed praising God, emerged untouched, and Nebuchadnezzar promoted them.

l: Azarias, Daniel (Greek)
s: Azarias, also called Azariah, is a companion of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. Standing in the fire, he prays, blessing the Lord, confessing Israel's sins as just judgment, and asking deliverance; the Lord's angel then descends into the furnace with him and his fellows.

l: golden image, Daniel (Greek)
s: A gold image sixty cubits high and six wide, set up by Nebuchadnezzar on the plain of Dura. Officials attended its dedication, all peoples were commanded to worship it at music's sound, but Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego refused.

l: burning fiery furnace, Daniel (Greek)
s: is_located_in Babylon [punishment for those who do not worship the image] The furnace was the punishment decreed for anyone who did not worship the golden image. It was heated seven times more than usual, and its flame killed the men who threw in the three, streamed out forty nine cubits above it, and burned Chaldeans around it. Inside, the angel made it like a moist whistling wind, and the fire did not touch the three men.

l: angel of the Lord, Daniel (Greek)
s: protects Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego [delivered them in the furnace] The angel of the Lord came down into the furnace together with Azarias and his fellows and struck the flame out of the furnace. He made the midst of it like a moist whistling wind, so the fire neither hurt nor troubled the three men. Nebuchadnezzar later said God had sent his angel to deliver his servants.

l: tree (in Nebuchadnezzar's dream), Daniel (Greek)
s: A great tree in Nebuchadnezzar's dream, standing mid-earth with sky-high height, beautiful leaves, and fruit feeding all, sheltering animals and birds. A watcher orders it cut down, leaving a stump bound in iron and bronze; Daniel identifies it as Nebuchadnezzar, symbolizing his greatness and dominion.

l: dream (Nebuchadnezzar's dream), Daniel (Greek)
s: Nebuchadnezzar's frightening dream, received on his bed, shows a great tree and a holy watcher descending from the sky to decree the tree's felling and a man's heart changed to an animal's for seven times, so the living know the Most High rules; only Daniel can interpret it.

l: interpretation of the dream (Daniel's), Daniel (Greek)
s: Daniel's interpretation of the dream identifies the tree as Nebuchadnezzar, whose greatness reaches the sky and dominion the earth's end. It declares the Most High's decree: he will be driven from men, live with animals, eat grass and be dew-wet for seven times until he knows heaven rules; the stump signifies his kingdom's restoration.

l: Nebuchadnezzar's madness and humbling, Daniel (Greek)
s: Nebuchadnezzar's madness and humbling is an event caused by his pride in boasting of Babylon. A sky voice declares his kingdom departed; immediately he is driven from men, eats grass like oxen, and grows feather-like hair and claw-like nails. It ends when he looks to heaven and his understanding and kingdom are restored.

l: Belshazzar, Daniel (Greek)
s: Belshazzar, a Chaldean king of Babylon and son of Nebuchadnezzar, has not humbled his heart and praises idol gods. He holds a great feast using temple vessels, is terrified by the writing on the wall, rewards Daniel for reading it with purple and third rulership, and is slain that same night.

l: Darius the Mede, Daniel (Greek)
s: Darius the Mede, son of Ahasuerus and of Median descent, receives Belshazzar's kingdom at about sixty-two and is made king over the Chaldeans. He appoints one hundred twenty governors and three presidents, planning to elevate Daniel. Tricked into signing the thirty-day decree, he is bound by the law and has Daniel cast into the den, fasting overnight. Finding Daniel alive, he rejoices, punishes the accusers, and decrees that all must fear Daniel's God.

l: Belshazzar's feast, Daniel (Greek)
s: has_attendees a thousand lords The feast is a great banquet for a thousand lords at which the king drinks wine before them. It features the use of the temple vessels by the king, his lords, wives, and concubines, and the praise of gods of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood, and stone. It is interrupted by the appearance of the hand writing on the wall.

l: writing on the wall, Daniel (Greek)
s: Writing on a palace wall's plaster near the lamp stand, reading MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN. No wise man can read it; Daniel reads it, interpreting God numbering and ending the kingdom, weighing the king wanting, dividing it to Medes and Persians.

l: hand that wrote, Daniel (Greek)
s: A man's hand's fingers, sent from before Most High God, appear during the feast's blasphemy and write on the palace wall before the king; Daniel explains its divine origin and inscription.

l: Belshazzar's kingdom, Daniel (Greek)
s: Belshazzar's kingdom is a Chaldean realm that Daniel interprets as counted and ended by God, then divided and given to the Medes and Persians; that night Belshazzar is slain and Darius the Mede receives it.

l: presidents and local governors, Daniel (Greek)
s: The presidents and local governors, accountable to King Darius, oppose Daniel. Finding no fault in him, they target his God's law, trick Darius into the thirty-day decree, accuse Daniel after seeing him pray, and are finally cast with their families into the lions' den and killed.

l: royal decree (Darius's thirty-day decree), Daniel (Greek)
s: A royal decree signed by Darius, proposed by the presidents and governors, forbids petitioning any god or man except the king for thirty days, on penalty of the lions' den. Bound by the unalterable law of the Medes and Persians, Darius cannot revoke it, leading to Daniel's being thrown into the den.

l: den of lions, Daniel (Greek)
s: has_part stone (sealing the den) [sealed with signets of the king and his lords] The den of lions is the punishment place named in the decree. Daniel is cast into it, a stone is laid on its mouth and sealed with the signets of the king and his lords, and Daniel is taken up out of it unharmed. The accusers and their families are then thrown into it.

l: lions, Daniel (Greek)
s: The lions' mouths are shut by God's angel, so they do not hurt Daniel overnight. When Daniel's accusers, with their children and wives, are cast in, the lions maul them and break all their bones before they reach the bottom of the den.

l: Cyrus the Persian, Daniel (Greek)
s: Cyrus the Persian receives the kingdom after Astyages is gathered to his fathers, honors Daniel, and at first worships Bel and believes it is a living god. After Daniel exposes the priests, he kills them and gives Bel to Daniel, but later yields to the Babylonians' threats and delivers Daniel to them. On finding Daniel alive in the den, he praises the Lord, the God of Daniel, and has Daniel's accusers thrown to the lions.

l: Daniel's prayer, Daniel (Greek)
s: Daniel's prayer is a thrice-daily act of petition, supplication and thanks to his God, kneeling toward Jerusalem with windows open, continued despite the decree; the men find him praying, grounding their accusation.

l: Ancient of Days, Daniel (Greek)
s: The Ancient of Days is a majestic judge with snow-white clothing and wool-like hair, enthroned on fiery wheeled flames. Attended by countless servants, he opens the books, sets judgment, and gives judgment to the saints when the son of man comes.

l: one like a son of man, Daniel (Greek)
s: receives everlasting kingdom [dominion, glory; all peoples serve him] One like a son of man comes with the clouds and is brought near before the Ancient of Days. He is given dominion, glory and a kingdom so that all peoples, nations and languages serve him. His dominion is everlasting and his kingdom will not be destroyed.

l: saints of the Most High, Daniel (Greek)
s: possesses everlasting kingdom [forever] The saints are warred against and prevailed over by the little horn, and are worn out by him until a time, times and half a time. Then judgment is given to them and they receive and possess the kingdom forever. The greatness of the kingdoms under the whole sky is given to the people of the saints.

l: Daniel's dream and visions, Daniel (Greek)
s: The dream comes by night in the first year of Belshazzar and is written down by Daniel. It shows four animals from the sea, a little horn, the Ancient of Days in judgment, and one like a son of man receiving an everlasting kingdom. An attendant interprets it, and it leaves Daniel troubled.

l: first animal (lion with eagle's wings), Daniel (Greek)
s: The first animal resembles a lion with eagle's wings; its wings are plucked, it is lifted from the earth to stand on two feet like a man, and receives a man's heart.

l: second animal (bear), Daniel (Greek)
s: The second animal resembles a bear, raised on one side, holding three ribs between its teeth, and is commanded to arise and devour much flesh.

l: third animal (leopard), Daniel (Greek)
s: The third animal, leopard-like with four bird's wings and four heads, is introduced in Chapter 7 and is finally given dominion.

l: fourth animal, Daniel (Greek)
s: The fourth animal is an awesome, exceedingly strong beast with great iron teeth, bronze nails and ten horns, differing from all others. It devours and tramples, is interpreted as a fourth kingdom devouring the whole earth, and is finally slain, destroyed and burned with fire.

l: four great animals, Daniel (Greek)
s: Four great animals, each different from the others, rise from the great sea after the four winds break out on it. They are interpreted as four kings arising from the earth; the remaining animals lose dominion but live on briefly.

l: ten horns, Daniel (Greek)
s: is_a ten kings [arise out of the fourth kingdom] The fourth animal has ten horns, which are interpreted as ten kings who will arise out of its kingdom. Three of the horns are plucked up by the roots before the little horn.

l: little horn, Daniel (Greek)
s: A little horn arises among ten horns, uprooting three. With human-like eyes and a mouth speaking great things, it wars against the saints and prevails until the Ancient of Days comes. Interpreted as a king, it speaks against the Most High, wears out saints, plans to change times and law, and is finally destroyed.

l: thrones and judgment, Daniel (Greek)
s: has books [opened when judgment was set] Thrones are placed and the Ancient of Days sits, with a fiery stream flowing from before him and the books opened. Judgment is set, the horn's great words are answered, and the fourth animal is slain. Judgment is given to the saints, and the little horn's dominion is taken away to be consumed and destroyed to the end.

l: ram (vision of the two-horned ram), Daniel (Greek)
s: In Chapter 8's vision, a two-horned ram, the higher horn rising last, pushes westward, northward and southward. Nothing can stand before it, and it acts as it wills and magnifies itself. A male goat then breaks its horns and tramples it, with no deliverer. Gabriel explains the ram is the kings of Media and Persia.
